8 min read
Just now

--

I’m 18, and 40 days ago I had never opened a pull request. Here’s the exact method I used to pick a repo — and what your first PR actually feels like.
Press enter or click to view image in full size

The one line that sent me to GitHub at midnight
I was half-watching a YouTube video when someone said that open source can completely change how you think about software engineering.
I don’t remember the channel. I don’t remember the video. I remember the line.
I didn’t announce anything. No “Day 1 of my open source journey” post, no telling my friends. I just wanted to find out whether the line was true.
Let me be honest about the other reason, because everyone has it and nobody admits it: there’s a certain status in being the person who contributes to open source. If you’re young, that status is very real — every class has one guy who contributes to real projects, and if people find out, that’s the only thing they talk about. It’s a nice side effect. It is not a reason. A reason has to survive week three, when you’re reading 4,000 lines of somebody else’s code at 1 a.m. and none of it makes sense. Curiosity survives that. Status doesn’t.
The hard part isn’t contributing. It’s choosing.
Every tutorial tells you to “start contributing to open source.” Almost none of them tell you where.
So you open GitHub, search “good first issue,” and get hit with the real beginner problem: hundreds of millions of repositories, issues that were claimed eight months ago and never closed, projects whose last commit was in 2021, and maintainers who never reply. You bounce between five repos in one evening and contribute to none of them.
That’s where I was. Here’s what got me out of it.
Step 1: Three questions, on paper, before you open GitHub
Get a notebook and a pen. Actually write the answers — typing them doesn’t work the same way, and you’ll need them in Step 2.
1. Which programming language am I genuinely good at? Not learning. Not “did a course in.” Good at. If you can’t debug in it without Googling the syntax, it doesn’t go on the list.
2. If I had to build one polished project from scratch — a real one, not a school assignment — what would it be, and what stack would I use? This is the question that quietly tells you your domain. If your answer involves dataframes and model training, your repo lives in the ML tooling world. If it involves routes and auth, it lives somewhere else entirely. Write down the frameworks and libraries by name.
3. How many hours a week can I realistically give this — for three months, not for one excited weekend? Be brutal here. I would rather you write “6 hours” and mean it than write “40 hours” and disappear after ten days. Maintainers notice who comes back. Consistency is the entire currency of open source, and it’s the one thing you can offer on day one that has nothing to do with skill.
Step 2: Turn your answers into one search prompt
Now open GitHub, open Copilot (ChatGPT or Claude work identically), and paste this in — filling the brackets with what you just wrote:
I’m looking for an open source organization to contribute to. Find projects that meet all of these criteria: at least 50 stars, well-regarded in [your field], built in [your language], using frameworks or libraries like [your frameworks], and actively accepting new contributors. For each one, tell me the last commit date and how quickly recent pull requests were reviewed.
This is exactly what I typed, minus the placeholders:
I’m looking for an open source organization to contribute to. Find projects that meet all of these criteria: at least 50 stars, well-regarded in the data/ML space, built in Python or Rust, using frameworks or libraries like pandas, TensorFlow or scikit-learn, and actively accepting new contributors.
Now you see why Step 1 mattered. Without those three answers, that prompt is empty.
Don’t trust the list blindly. The model will hand you ten repos and some of them will be dead. Open each one and check four things — it takes ninety seconds per repo:

• Last commit: within the past 30 days. Older than that and you’ll be waiting forever for a review.

• Open pull requests: are recent ones getting comments within a week? Open two and read the review threads.

• A CONTRIBUTING.md that actually exists and explains how to set the project up locally.

• The tone in the issues. Read three issue threads. You will know within a minute whether beginners get helped or ignored.
That last one matters more than the star count, and nobody tells you that.
Why I picked DataLoom
I ended up at DataLoom, a data cleaning and transformation tool under the c2siorg organization. It passed all four checks, it sat exactly in the domain I’d written on paper, and it was small enough that I could eventually hold most of it in my head — which, for a first project, matters far more than prestige.
I made my first contribution on 15 June 2026. It’s now 25 July, and I have 8 merged pull requests across DataLoom and its sibling project, TensorMap.
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Nothing glamorous, either. A case-sensitivity bug in string filtering. Hover tooltips on toolbar icons. A dark mode fix where a panel was still using hardcoded light-theme classes. Then bigger things: a preview-before-apply flow rolled out across all twelve transformation forms, and a CI change that split the lint workflow so untrusted pull request code stops running with write permissions.
You don’t start at the CI security fix. You start at the tooltip. That’s the whole point.
What actually happens when you open your first pull request
Here’s the part I wish someone had walked me through, minute by minute.
You open the repo and feel like the dumbest person alive. Everyone else’s PRs look surgical. There are acronyms in the issue titles you’ve never seen. This feeling is not a signal. Every single person in that contributors list felt it, and most of them still do on a new codebase.
You fork it, clone it, and try to run it locally. This alone will eat your first evening — mine involved Docker Compose, a Postgres container, and a missing environment variable that took an hour to find. When it finally boots, that’s your first real win, and it’s a bigger one than it feels like.
You find a bug. A small one. A real one. You open an issue and write, “Can I work on this?”
Someone replies: “Go ahead, it’s yours.” I’m going to try to describe this one instead of skipping it, because it’s the moment everything turns: a stranger with commit rights on a project you admire just handed you a piece of it, in public, with your username attached. That’s not encouragement. That’s permission — and it’s oddly heavier than encouragement.
You write the fix in forty minutes and spend three hours on the commit message. Then you hit “Create pull request” with roughly a million thoughts in your head, most of them about how it’s going to look when they reject it.
And then: nothing. Hours. Sometimes days. This is the stage that breaks people, so read the next section carefully.
Then a comment: “needs revision.” You’ll read it as rejection. It isn’t. A maintainer spent part of their evening reading code written by someone they’ve never met, and cared enough to tell you how to make it better. That’s the most under-appreciated gift in this entire ecosystem. You push a fix in ten minutes and start waiting again.
Then the icon turns purple. Merged.
Your code — the code you wrote on your laptop, in your room, while doubting every line of it — is now running on the machines of people who will never know your name. I’m not going to try to name that feeling. Go get it, then come tell me in the comments what it was like for you. That’s the part of these articles I actually read.
The waiting is normal. Read this before you panic.
Maintainers are volunteers. They have jobs, degrees, families, and a review queue. A few hours to a few days is completely normal, and silence is almost never about you.
Two rules that fixed this for me:

• Never wait idle. The moment a PR goes up, open the next issue. If you’re always three issues deep, review latency stops being emotionally expensive.

• Ping once, politely, after a week. “Hi, just checking whether this needs anything from my side.” That’s it. That’s the whole message.
The thing I didn’t expect: nobody judged me
The biggest fear every new contributor carries is looking stupid in public. It’s a permanent, searchable, screenshot-able kind of public, too.
Forty days in, here’s what actually happened: I asked beginner questions and got real answers. I proposed a feature, had another contributor push back with a better-reasoned design, and changed direction — and the whole exchange was completely free of condescension. Last week I reviewed somebody else’s PR for the first time and raised two issues with their approach; they fixed one immediately and documented the other as a follow-up.
Nobody once made me feel like I was in the way. That’s not luck — that’s what a healthy project looks like, and it’s exactly what you’re screening for when you read those issue threads in Step 2.
Those people are the reason I’m still contributing. The person who commented “go ahead” on my first issue and the maintainer who merged my first PR have no idea they did anything. They did everything.
So, has open source changed my life?
I don’t know yet. That’s the honest answer, and I’m not going to pretend otherwise 40 days in.
Here’s what I can measure:

• I can read a large codebase I didn’t write and find my way around it.

• I can take a review comment without my ego getting involved.

• I’ve been wrong in public, in writing, in front of better engineers — and nothing bad happened.

• I have a public record of real work, which at 18 with no CS degree is worth considerably more than another certificate.
That’s not “life-changing” yet. It’s more than I had in May.
Part two of this article gets written the day I can answer the question properly. Until then: keep contributing — or start.
Your turn
If this is the article that gets you to open your first pull request, I want to know. Drop a comment with:

• the repo you picked, and

• what that “merged” notification actually felt like.
I want this comment section to be the thing I didn’t have when I started — a pile of first-PR stories from people who were exactly as terrified as you are right now.
